lines.content: description: Apply the SE-EDU Git commit message conventions to this project.

Apply the SE-EDU Git conventions to all future commits. Every commit must have a clear subject in imperative mood, start with a capital letter, contain no final period, and ideally be at most 50 characters (hard limit 72 characters). A scope or category may be used when helpful.
For non-trivial changes, add a body separated from the subject by a blank line, wrap it at 72 characters, and explain what changed and why. Use bullet points when they improve clarity.
description: Apply the SE-EDU intermediate Java coding conventions to this project.

Apply the SE-EDU Java basic and intermediate conventions to all Java code in this project. Use the project name as the root package and keep package names lower case. Use PascalCase nouns for classes, camelCase verbs for methods, camelCase variables, and SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants.

Use four-space indentation, K&R braces, consistent explicit imports, and keep lines within 120 characters. Use braces for all loop and conditional bodies, and make intentional switch fall-through explicit.

Write descriptive JavaDoc header comments for all public classes and methods. Include `@param`, `@return`, and `@throws` when useful. Comments must be in English using American spelling. Test methods may use `featureUnderTest_testScenario_expectedBehavior()`.

This repository is a starter template for a greenfield Java project used in an introductory software engineering course in an undergraduate computer science program. Students use it as the starting point for their own projects.

Unless the user says otherwise, assume that you are assisting a student working on a project in this repository. If the user identifies themselves as an instructor or another project stakeholder, adapt your response to that role.
* Prior knowledge: Basic Java and OOP concepts.
* Level of programming experience: [to be filled]
* IDE and level of expertise: [to be filled]
* Explain the rationale for significant actions: what you did and why.
* Keep explanations brief but instructive, supporting learning through responsible use of AI. For example:
* When suggesting a Git command, briefly explain what it does.
* Add explanatory Javadoc comments to all classes and to nontrivial methods and fields when their purpose or behavior is not obvious.
* Make generated code as self-explanatory as possible, and include explanatory comments where they improve understanding.
* When faced with a design choice, choose the simplest option that is sufficient for the requirements, while briefly explaining relevant more advanced alternatives.

All Java code must follow `.codex/skills/seedu-java-coding-standard/SKILL.md`, based on the SE-EDU intermediate Java conventions. Use the lower-case package structure, explicit imports, four-space indentation, a 120-character line limit, and descriptive JavaDoc for public classes and methods.

All future commits must follow `.codex/skills/seedu-git-standard/SKILL.md`, based on the SE-EDU Git conventions. Use imperative, capitalized subjects without a final period, keep them within the recommended length, and include a concise WHAT/WHY body for non-trivial changes.

Maintain JUnit tests for approximately the highest-value 50% of the codebase's methods, prioritizing core business logic, complex validation, and critical behavior. Update the relevant JUnit tests after every code change so that the test coverage target remains satisfied.
Ensure that Java 25 is used when running the application or build tasks. On macOS, use `sdk use java 25.0.3.fx-zulu` to switch to Java 25 if needed.
Use lightweight tags unless the user requests an annotated tag.
When proposing or creating a commit message, include enough detail to explain the rationale for the change.
Do not commit or push unless explicitly asked.

Tabby is a lightweight task manager for todos, deadlines, and events. It is available as a command-line application and a JavaFX graphical interface.
- View all tasks or search by keyword
- Mark tasks done, undo completion, and delete tasks
- Use a responsive GUI with quick-action buttons
The GUI opens with a command field. Type a command and press **Enter** or click **Run**. Select a task to use the quick-action buttons.
For the command-line interface, run the `ip.Tabby` application from your IDE or build configuration.
| `find KEYWORD` | Shows tasks whose descriptions contain the keyword |
| `event DESCRIPTION /from START /to END` | Adds an event |
| `mark NUMBER` | Marks a task as done |
| `unmark NUMBER` | Marks a task as not done |
Task numbers are shown by `list` and beside each task in the GUI. For example:
Tabby accepts dates in `yyyy-MM-dd` or `d/M/yyyy` format. Date-times can use `yyyy-MM-dd HHmm`, `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm`, `d/M/yyyy HHmm`, or `d/M/yyyy HH:mm`.
An event must start before it ends. Invalid dates such as February 30, missing values, and duplicate `/by`, `/from`, or `/to` clauses are rejected with an explanatory error.

If a command is incomplete or has an invalid task number, Tabby keeps existing tasks and shows an error. Tasks are saved in `data/tabby.txt` after changes. If the file does not exist, Tabby starts with an empty list and creates the file when you add your first task.
- Use `help` whenever you forget a command format.
- Use `list` to refresh the complete task list after a search.
- In the GUI, use **Mark done**, **Unmark**, and **Delete** after selecting a task.
